chapters.chapter_title: Orienting Yourself: The Use of Coordinates

image_asset.title: 2D Cartesian Coordinate Plane showing axes, origin O(0,0), four quadrants, and plotted points P(3,4) & Q(-3,-4).

hotspots.label: Origin O(0,0)
hotspots.tooltip: Point of perpendicular intersection of x and y axes.

hotspots.label: Quadrant I (+,+)
hotspots.tooltip: Region where both abscissa x > 0 and ordinate y > 0.

hotspots.label: Quadrant III (-,-)
hotspots.tooltip: Region where both abscissa x < 0 and ordinate y < 0.

sections.content: Urban layouts in the Sindhu-Sarasvatī Civilisation (Harappa and Mohenjo-daro) featured planned grid systems with streets intersecting at right angles. Baudhāyana's Śhulbasūtras (c. 800 BCE) defined perpendicular reference lines—Prāchī (east-west axis) and Tiryak (north-south axis)—to construct Vedic altars (Vedis). René Descartes later formalized two-dimensional coordinate geometry.
key_takeaways: Prāchī and Tiryak were ancient Indian orthogonal reference lines.
Orthogonal grids allow unambiguous spatial positioning.

sections.content: A 2D Cartesian plane is defined by two perpendicular axes: the horizontal x-axis and vertical y-axis intersecting at Origin O(0,0). Every point P is defined by an ordered pair (x, y), where x is the abscissa (distance from y-axis) and y is the ordinate (distance from x-axis). The axes divide the plane into 4 quadrants: QI (+,+), QII (-,+), QIII (-,-), and QIV (+,-).
key_takeaways: Points on x-axis have y = 0, expressed as (x, 0).
Points on y-axis have x = 0, expressed as (0, y).

sections.content: The distance between P1(x1, y1) and P2(x2, y2) is derived using the Baudhāyana-Pythagoras theorem: d = sqrt((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2). The distance from origin O(0,0) is d = sqrt(x^2 + y^2). Midpoint M is M = ((x1+x2)/2, (y1+y2)/2). Reflecting (x, y) across x-axis gives (x, -y); across y-axis gives (-x, y).
key_takeaways: Distance d is always non-negative.
Section and trisection formulas divide line segments in given ratios.

image_asset.title: Straight line graph of linear polynomial y = ax + b showing slope right triangle and y-intercept.

hotspots.label: Slope (a = Rise/Run)
hotspots.tooltip: Rate of change measuring line steepness.

hotspots.label: y-intercept (0, b)
hotspots.tooltip: Point where line crosses vertical y-axis.

sections.content: A linear polynomial in variable x is a univariate polynomial of degree 1 having general form p(x) = ax + b, where a != 0. Here 'a' is the coefficient of x, and 'b' is the constant term. The zero of polynomial p(x) is the value x = -b/a where p(x) = 0.
key_takeaways: Degree 1 means the highest exponent of x is 1.
A linear polynomial has exactly one real zero at x = -b/a.

sections.section_number_and_title: 2.2 Constant First Differences, Linear Growth & Decay
sections.content: In an input-output data table with uniform x-step increments delta_x, a constant first difference delta_y indicates linear behavior. Linear growth occurs when quantity increases steadily (slope a > 0, e.g. C(x) = 15x + 50). Linear decay occurs when quantity decreases steadily (slope a < 0, e.g. W(t) = 500 - 25t).
key_takeaways: Constant rate of change delta_y / delta_x defines linear functions.
Linear growth slants upward; linear decay slants downward.

sections.section_number_and_title: 2.3 Graphical Properties: Slope, Intercepts & Parallel Lines
sections.content: The graph of y = ax + b is always a straight line. Slope 'a' measures steepness (rise / run). The y-intercept 'b' is the point (0, b) where the line crosses the y-axis. Two lines with equal slopes a1 = a2 but different intercepts b1 != b2 are parallel and never intersect.
key_takeaways: Slope a = (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1).
Parallel lines share identical slope 'a'.

sections.section_number_and_title: 3.1 Hierarchy of Number Sets & Continuous Number Line
sections.content: Numbers evolved from counting tallies to Natural numbers N, Whole numbers W, Integers Z, Rational numbers Q (p/q, q != 0), and Irrational numbers Q' (non-terminating non-repeating decimals). Together Q and Q' form Real numbers R, filling every point on the continuous real number line. Between any two real numbers lie infinitely many rational and irrational numbers.
key_takeaways: N subset of W subset of Z subset of Q subset of R.
Real line R = Q union Q'.

sections.section_number_and_title: 3.2 Decimal Expansions: Terminating, Recurring & Cyclic Numbers
sections.content: A rational number p/q has a terminating decimal expansion if and only if prime factors of q are purely of form 2^m * 5^n. Otherwise it forms a non-terminating periodic repeating decimal. Cyclic decimals like 1/7 = 0.142857142857... exhibit rotating digit blocks for multiples 2/7, 3/7, etc.
key_takeaways: Terminating decimals require q = 2^m * 5^n.
Recurring decimals can be converted to p/q form using algebraic subtraction.

sections.section_number_and_title: 3.3 Irrationality Proofs, Wheel of Theodorus & Infinite Series
sections.content: Proof of sqrt(2) irrationality uses proof by contradiction with prime factor parity. The Wheel of Theodorus (Square Root Spiral) geometrically constructs hypotenuses sqrt(2), sqrt(3), sqrt(4)... using right triangles with unit legs. Mādhava of Saṅgamagrāma derived the infinite series pi/4 = 1 - 1/3 + 1/5 - 1/7 + ...
key_takeaways: sqrt(p) is irrational for any prime p.
Mādhava series provides rational approximations converging to pi.

image_asset.title: Area decomposition proof of identity (a+b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2 using partitioned square regions.

hotspots.label: Square a^2
hotspots.tooltip: Primary square region of side length a.

hotspots.label: Rectangles 2ab
hotspots.tooltip: Two congruent side rectangles each having area a * b.

sections.content: Identities hold true for all variable values. Binomial square (a+b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2 is proven geometrically by area decomposition of a square into two sub-squares and two rectangles. Difference of squares: a^2 - b^2 = (a-b)(a+b). Trinomial square: (a+b+c)^2 = a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + 2ab + 2bc + 2ca. Śhrīdharāchārya's method a^2 = (a+b)(a-b) + b^2 enables mental squaring.
key_takeaways: Śhrīdharāchārya method simplifies mental arithmetic.

sections.content: Cube expansion (a+b)^3 = a^3 + b^3 + 3ab(a+b) decomposes geometrically into 2 cubes and 6 rectangular prisms. Sum of cubes: a^3 + b^3 = (a+b)(a^2 - ab + b^2); Difference of cubes: a^3 - b^3 = (a-b)(a^2 + ab + b^2). Conditional Identity: If a + b + c = 0, then a^3 + b^3 + c^3 = 3abc.
key_takeaways: Volume decomposition visually proves cubic expansions.
Conditional identity 3abc applies whenever a+b+c=0.

sections.content: Quadratic polynomials ax^2 + bx + c are factorised by splitting middle term b into p + q where p+q = b and p*q = a*c. Factor Theorem states that (x - r) is a factor of p(x) if and only if p(r) = 0.
key_takeaways: p(r) = 0 implies (x - r) is a factor.
Splitting middle term converts quadratics to grouped factors.

chapters.chapter_title: I’m Up and Down, and Round and Round

image_asset.title: Circle diagram demonstrating Inscribed Angle Theorem and Cyclic Quadrilateral supplementary angles.

hotspots.label: Central Angle AOB
hotspots.tooltip: Angle subtended by arc AB at centre O (double the inscribed angle).

hotspots.label: Inscribed Angle ACB
hotspots.tooltip: Angle subtended by arc AB on the major circumference.

sections.content: A circle is the locus of points equidistant from fixed centre O. A perpendicular dropped from centre O to chord AB bisects the chord (AM = MB). Equal chords are equidistant from centre. Exactly one circumcircle passes through 3 non-collinear points; its centre is the circumcentre.
key_takeaways: Perpendicular from centre bisects chord.
Circumcentre is intersection of side perpendicular bisectors.

sections.content: Inscribed Angle Theorem: Central angle angle AOB = 2 * angle ACB (inscribed angle on circumference). Angles subtended in the same segment of a circle are equal. Angle subtended in a semicircle is a right angle (90 degrees).
key_takeaways: Central angle is double the inscribed angle.
Angle in semicircle = 90 deg.

sections.content: A quadrilateral is cyclic if all 4 vertices touch a circle. Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary: angle A + angle C = 180 degrees. Converse: if opposite angles sum to 180 degrees, the quadrilateral is cyclic.
key_takeaways: Cyclic quad: angle A + angle C = 180 deg.
Concyclicity holds when opposite angles are supplementary.

image_asset.title: Mensuration overview displaying circular sector, segment, and concentric stadium running track.

hotspots.label: Circular Sector
hotspots.tooltip: Region bounded by two radii and central arc theta.

hotspots.label: Running Track Ring
hotspots.tooltip: Area between outer radius R and inner radius r: pi*(R^2 - r^2).

sections.content: Parallelogram Area = base * height; Triangle Area = 1/2 * base * height; Trapezium Area = 1/2 * (sum of parallel sides) * height. Brahmagupta's formula for cyclic quadrilateral area = sqrt((s-a)(s-b)(s-c)(s-d)) where s = (a+b+c+d)/2.
key_takeaways: Trapezium Area = 1/2 * (a + b) * h.
Brahmagupta formula generalizes Heron's formula to cyclic quadrilaterals.

sections.content: For a triangle with side lengths a, b, c and semi-perimeter s = (a+b+c)/2, Area = sqrt(s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)). For an equilateral triangle of side 'a', Area = (sqrt(3)/4) * a^2.
key_takeaways: Heron's formula computes area without needing explicit height.
Equilateral Area = (sqrt(3)/4) * a^2.

sections.section_number_and_title: 6.3 Circular Regions: Sectors, Segments & Track Geometry
sections.content: Circumference C = 2*pi*r; Circle Area = pi*r^2. Arc Length L = (theta/360) * 2*pi*r; Sector Area = (theta/360) * pi*r^2. Minor Segment Area = Sector Area - Triangle Area. Running track path area between outer R and inner r = pi*(R^2 - r^2).
key_takeaways: Sector Area = (theta/360) * pi * r^2.
Segment Area = Sector Area - Triangle Area.

chapters.chapter_title: The Mathematics of Maybe: Introduction to Probability

image_asset.title: Tree diagram for 2-coin tosses and geometric probability target board.

hotspots.label: Coin Tree Branches
hotspots.tooltip: Branching paths representing sample space outcomes {HH, HT, TH, TT}.

hotspots.label: Geometric Target Ring
hotspots.tooltip: Ratio of target circle area to enclosing square board area.

sections.content: A random experiment has known possible outcomes, but individual trial results are unpredictable. Probability P(E) lies strictly between 0 and 1: 0 <= P(E) <= 1. P(Impossible) = 0; P(Certain) = 1. Complementary events: P(E) + P(not E) = 1.
key_takeaways: P(not E) = 1 - P(E).

sections.section_number_and_title: 7.2 Experimental vs Theoretical Probability & Law of Large Numbers
sections.content: Empirical probability P_exp(E) = (favorable trials) / (total trials). Theoretical probability P_th(E) = n(E) / n(S) assuming equally likely outcomes. Law of Large Numbers: relative frequency converges to theoretical probability as trial count n -> infinity (e.g. Karl Pearson's 24,000 coin flips).
key_takeaways: Empirical probability relies on trial data.
Law of Large Numbers guarantees convergence as n increases.

sections.content: Tree diagrams and coordinate matrices organize multi-stage sample spaces (2 coins: 4 outcomes; 2 dice: 36 outcomes). Geometric Probability = (Target Region Area) / (Total Enclosing Area).
key_takeaways: n(S) for 2 dice = 36.
Geometric probability evaluates area ratios.

chapters.chapter_title: Predicting What Comes Next: Exploring Sequences and Progressions

image_asset.title: Dot arrays for triangular numbers T_n and step plot for Arithmetic Progression.

hotspots.label: Triangular Dot Arrays
hotspots.tooltip: Pattern T_n = n(n+1)/2 forming square numbers when consecutive arrays combine.

hotspots.label: AP Step Plot
hotspots.tooltip: Constant step addition d = t_n - t_(n-1) forming a linear growth profile.

sections.section_number_and_title: 8.1 Pattern Rules, Triangular Numbers & Special Sequences
sections.content: Explicit rules compute term t_n directly from position n (e.g. t_n = 2n+1). Recursive rules compute t_n from preceding terms (e.g. t_n = t_(n-1) + d). Triangular numbers T_n = n(n+1)/2 satisfy T_n + T_(n-1) = n^2. Virahānka-Fibonacci sequence: V_1=1, V_2=1, V_n = V_(n-1) + V_(n-2).
key_takeaways: Explicit rule calculates directly; recursive uses prior term.

sections.content: An AP has constant common difference d = t_n - t_(n-1). Formula for nth term: t_n = a + (n-1)d. Sum of first n terms: S_n = (n/2)*[2a + (n-1)d] or S_n = (n/2)*[a + l].

A GP has constant common ratio r = t_n / t_(n-1). Formula for nth term: t_n = a * r^(n-1). AP models linear additive growth; GP models exponential multiplicative growth. Fractals like Sierpiński triangle exhibit GP self-similarity.
key_takeaways: GP models exponential growth.
